items_missed: Never asked 'how are you today?' — 'How can I help you out today?' is the service version, not the warm-up.
No agenda statement and no 'sound good?'. He is organized enough that the call had a de facto structure, but the customer was never told what was coming or how long it would take.

Not one address was captured on this call. No origin, no destination, no zip codes, nothing — and he booked the move. He knows the new place is a house, that it is five minutes away, and that the dining table stays on the first floor, which means he has the shape of the job and none of the coordinates. Everything downstream — trip fee applicability, drive time, crew dispatch — is riding on whatever the online form captured.

The reason for the call was never resolved. She opened with 'I did the online one and it said I needed to contact someone because it's involved square footage that too large I guess' — the form kicked her out on square footage — and Jack's response was 'so it we're just, is it just a one bedroom apartment?' He confirmed the small origin and never once asked the square footage of the destination house. The flag that generated this lead was never investigated, which is also the one variable that could break his six-hour estimate on the unload side.
Box count never asked. He quoted $100 in packing materials and built a packing-hours estimate without ever asking how many boxes the job produces.
Garage, storage unit, balcony and other additional rooms never asked at either end.
Storage stops never asked.

Parking, HOA, loading dock and truck access never asked at either address, and 'apartment to house' means both ends have real access questions. He did confirm the elevator at the origin, which is the one access item he caught.

Moving stressors never asked. The customer asked three anxious logistics questions in a row — what to do with furniture she is not keeping, what to do ahead of time, whether she has to be present — which is a customer telling you she is nervous, and none of it drew 'what are you most worried about?'
No 'pricing is super simple' opener. 'Well, let me already see the way that our pricing works' is the setup line without the framing.

What's-included list was asserted rather than itemized: 'we'll wrap everything and blankets and shrink wrap we'll disassemble bed frame is put them back together for you. Absolutely everything is included in that cost.' Gas, truck, taxes, tools and insurance were never named, which matters because 'absolutely everything' is exactly the kind of claim a competitor's itemized list beats.

No Worries Damage Coverage never mentioned. Zero insurance content on a call that booked — no $2,000, no 'repair, replace, or reimburse,' no 60¢/lb baseline. This is the largest single gap on an otherwise strong call, and she has a $600-ish dining table that took four men to move and a set of TVs.
On-Time Guarantee never mentioned, and he set a specific 8:30 AM start time — 'Cool. 8:30 AM start time work for you.' That is the natural home for it and it went by.

'Take a carload' never said, on a move that is five minutes away. The customer volunteered the distance herself ('Straight over and it's five minutes away') and she is paying for packing labor by the hour. Nothing on this board was closer to free money.

No 'does that make sense?' close on the prep block. He delivered a long, genuinely useful prep speech and ended it with the customer saying 'Okay, cool' rather than confirming she would actually do any of it.

No bolded-details framing on the confirmation email, and the reply ask was about booking rather than verifying: 'all you gotta do is respond to the email that I sent and then we can get you set up and scheduled.' On a call where he captured no addresses and never confirmed the name, 'reply if anything in there is wrong' was not optional.
Business hours and a direct phone number were never given.
Ecobox referral not made, on a customer who is buying roughly $100 of boxes and moving five minutes down the road — the single most referral-relevant setup in this batch.

Customer's name never used once. She introduced herself in her first sentence: 'Hi Jack! This is Allison.' It was never spoken again — and the lead record on this call is filed under Joseph Hendon, a mismatch Jack never noticed or reconciled. That is a data-hygiene problem on a booked job, not just a politeness miss.

Name capture is the weakest link in an otherwise clean booking: no last name, no email address confirmed out loud, no phone number read back — on a call where he committed to send a confirmation email and set a crew for a Saturday morning.
top_strength: Jack is the only rep on this board who quoted the rate the way the scorecard asks for it and then built an estimate that holds up under scrutiny. The rate framing is exactly right: 'on Saturdays or rates $103 per mover. So, two over team would be a $206 hourly rate.' Per mover, then per team, so the customer can see the math and understand what a third mover would cost — which matters, because he had just talked himself out of sending one. The clock section is a clean 4/4 delivered in a single fluid pass: 'it's just based on time that time starts when we actually arrive and start moving that time stops once we've delivered and set everything up at the new place. So there's a two and a half hour minimum and then anytime after the two and a half hour minimum is pro rated fifteen minutes at a time' — followed immediately by a real sense-check, 'Do you have any questions about the pricing or the process?' The estimate itself is the best-constructed one in the batch and it is arithmetically exact: three to four hours moving, two to three packing, six hours total, six hours at $206 plus $100 materials equals the $1,336 he quoted. He then deliberately framed the downside rather than the upside — 'if there's not too much to pack, it only takes us an hour we finish the whole move-in in four and a half or five hours. That's how much you paid for.' What makes it accurate rather than lucky is that he actively de-scoped it: he asked whether the kitchen was 'lots of glassware like, on every shelf in every cabinet, or is it a little bit more minimal,' learned she had already removed the fragile items, and landed at 'probably only about like, two ish hours a packing' instead of the padded number. He did the same on crew size, and against his own revenue: 'I don't want to send you three movers if it's not really warrant it cause it'll be more expensive and all that but obviously I wanna make sure that we can get everything.' The prep speech was substantial and customer-prompted, covering both labeling discipline and a genuinely clever unload-side tip — 'we have these large open top bins that will carry some miscellaneous items... if you wanted to start moving around some of the small things while we're unloading the furniture. Then you can save time.' And the close is the best on the board: he offered, she leaned in, and he closed it on the spot with the no-deposit differentiator doing the work — 'There's no deposits and there's no cancellation fees. If you ever decide you want to change a date or just hire a different company, there's no payment upfront, you don't pay anything until your move is actually been completed.' Then: 'If you'd like I can confirm it... So if you'd like to you want to book it now.' Booked, with a start time, a Meet Your Mover mention, and a day-of call promise, all inside eight minutes.
coaching_note: Jack has the strongest sales mechanics on this board and the weakest data capture, and the gap between the two is the whole coaching note. He booked a Saturday move — crew committed, 8:30 AM start, confirmation email promised — without a single address, without a last name, without reading back an email address, and without noticing that the caller identified herself as Allison while the lead record says Joseph Hendon. That mismatch on a booked job is a dispatch problem waiting to happen. Fix: before the pricing block, always, 'Let me get the two addresses and confirm the best email and cell for you' — thirty seconds, and it is the difference between a booking and a booking that actually runs. Second priority, and the highest-value content gap: zero insurance. Nothing. He booked a customer with a 600-pound dining table and multiple TVs and never said the words No Worries Damage Coverage, never said $2,000, never said repair-replace-or-reimburse, and never gave her the 60¢/lb comparison that makes it land. One sentence inside the included-in-the-rate list fixes it: 'and every move comes with No Worries Damage Coverage — up to $2,000 to repair, replace or reimburse accidental damage, where the industry standard is sixty cents a pound.' Third: two differentiators were sitting right in front of him. He set an 8:30 AM start and never mentioned the On-Time Guarantee. And she told him the new place is five minutes away while buying packing labor by the hour — the 'take a carload' tip belonged there and would have been worth more to her than anything else he said. His prep speech was genuinely good but it is all about organization and labeling; add the consolidation list and the carload line and it becomes a full 10/10 section instead of a half one. Estimate accuracy: log this one as a positive for the bottom-4 comparison work. He gave the typical range for the home size, used 'just to be safe' language once — 'we generally allocate, you know, just like extra time for packing just to be safe' — and then immediately did the opposite of padding: he probed the kitchen specifically, got the answer that the glassware was already gone, and revised his packing hours down rather than leaving the buffer in. He also volunteered the cheaper outcome twice without being asked. That is calibration behavior, and it is worth pulling the actual against on September 26th to see whether six hours held. One structural gap to watch: the whole reason this lead came to a human is that the online form flagged the square footage as too large, and he never asked the destination house's square footage. His estimate is built entirely on the one-bedroom origin. If that house is 2,600 square feet with a long walk from the driveway, the unload half of his six hours is wrong and nobody will know until move day.
phone_presence_notes: Confident, easy and visibly on the customer's side — 'Hey, you know I don't want to send you three movers if it's not really warrant it cause it'll be more expensive' is the kind of line that builds trust faster than warmth does, and she converted on the call with three separate 'thank you so much I really appreciate it' moments; held back from a 5 by never once using her name and by a register that stays efficient rather than personal, with no humor or rapport beat anywhere in the eight minutes.
